title: [AINews] LLMs can read & write neural network weights: "Weight Space Programming" cuts Autoresearch out of the RSI loop
summary: Amid a deepening bear market for AI/tech (worthy of dark humor ) with Anthropic bonds receiving a “junk” rating and OpenAI fundraise headlines , we continue to see very surprising capability finds in the community, such as today. The best way to put today’s blockbuster paper in context is to recall Karpathy’s autoresearch from a mere 8 months ago , which presaged a summer of recursive self improvement fears : Abstrac
body:
Amid a deepening bear market for AI/tech (worthy of dark humor ) with Anthropic bonds receiving a “junk” rating and OpenAI fundraise headlines , we continue to see very surprising capability finds in the community, such as today.

The best way to put today’s blockbuster paper in context is to recall Karpathy’s autoresearch from a mere 8 months ago , which presaged a summer of recursive self improvement fears :

Abstractly, the demonstration is that you can take a sufficiently smart model and through running a series of experiments across a compute cluster, train a model autonomously without human expertise or intervention. However, this is usually done by an involved process of writing PyTorch/Jax code and running compute and watching loss curves and reading evals and optimizing kernels and data and….

Well, last month’s guest Alex Zhang comes back to coauthor a MONSTER discovery: what if you just ask a smart model to directly read and edit the weights of a dumber model?

In ML this is the equivalent of not looking at source code, just directly seeing the 1’s and 0’s of ( very small ) compiled executables, and being able to 1) tell what they do , 2) oneshot-fix bugs given failed traces or, with 50 steps, improve in a general direction ( possible overstatement here ), 3) writing entire network weights from scratch in one shot , beating some independently trained models.

If you believe that LLMs can truly fit and simulate everything given enough parameters (and in fact, LLMs are increasingly better calculators as you grow in size), then something like this was in theory bound to happen, but it is surprising nevertheless to have the ability suddenly emerge, as an independent reproduction seems to already have found:

Of course the exact thing we are really modeling is some variant of mechanistic interpretability (which could be done by hand ), and right now unlikely to scale to more advanced tasks than simple games and RL policies, but the world has now gone from 0 to 1 on this very new RSI capability…. which will immediately put to use and explored due to its remarkable efficiency.

AI News for 10/31/2026-11/02/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies!

DeepSeek Open-Sources a "Super-agent" Harness Prototype

Release : DeepSeek Harness published a long design article ( article ) and the dsh-superagent-prototype repo ( repo link ). An official English version followed ( @tianyi ).

Architecture : One long-lived router session talks to humans and hands out work. Isolated workers run tasks in parallel, triggered by GitHub events ( summary ).

Claimed results : In DeepSeek's own test, p95 completion time fell from 29.5 to 15.7 min versus a single session using subagents ( summary ).

Design rationale from a reviewer : Final reviewer 崔添翼 (@tianyi) says "Super" means a layer above the working agent, not superior intelligence. He frames the core trade-off as cross-task continuity versus throughput ( Zhihu summary ).

Stated limits : The harness has no built-in cross-session long-term memory yet. Separating state, compute and environment is mostly unimplemented. The prototype has only been validated in a small, trusted internal environment, and security, privacy and agent-to-agent communication remain open questions.

Prior art : He acknowledges that other teams explored similar architectures months earlier.

Practitioner reception : @badlogicgames says the design matches where Earendil is heading: a single long-lived entity, ad-hoc recursive delegation and cross-system event triggers. @omarsar0 calls it a "masterclass" in coordination-execution harness design. DeepSeek also says it aims to support pi and other major harnesses with each model generation ( @tianyi ).

Critique : @teortaxesTex calls the write-up "something of a hot mess." He argues DeepSeek builds internal crutches around model weaknesses such as hallucination rather than making the system generally robust. He also notes Bloomberg covered a repo that had no English announcement ( post ).

V4.1 naming confusion : A Renmin University FlashRSI README referenced deepseek-v4.1-pro , which prompted release speculation. Teortaxes says it is a placeholder: the real config uses v4-flash and v4-pro, and deepseek-v4.1-flash is not a valid ID ( thread , follow-up ). He also says the API fingerprints for V4.1F-1017 are unchanged ( fingerprints ).

Independent Evals and Frontier Model Signals

GDPx benchmark (SemiAnalysis) : The benchmark covers 206 agentic tasks across 11 economically valuable domains, including chip design, SWE, finance and biology. The best model scores only 12% ( launch ).

Results : Opus 5.5 leads at 12%. Gemini 4 Carbon is close behind at 10.9% at roughly 4x lower cost ( breakdown ).

Reactions : @dylan522p apologized to Google, calling Carbon "spikier" but very strong in some areas. @demishassabis welcomed the benchmark.

Analysis : @eliebakouch finds that removing safeguard-affected benchmarks changes the picture. In that view Carbon stays cheap, and Sol 6.1 is cheaper still. He also suggests OpenAI has stronger bio safeguards than Anthropic ( note ).

Within-family comparison : Sol 6.1 and Astra score very similarly, Carbon beats Argon across the board, and Sonnet is strong at SWE ( comparison ).

Possible bug : Some Argon cybersecurity runs may be affected by an Antigravity bug ( report ).

Audit concerns : One satirical post complains that GDPx is not open source and is costly to audit ( post ).

Epoch Capabilities Index : DeepSeek V4.1F-1017 scores 159, equal to GPT 5.5. That is 3 points above V4.1F-0910 and 10 above V4-Pro; Astra sits roughly 10 points higher ( @teortaxesTex ).

Gap to Mythos : @scaling01 notes that no Chinese model has matched Mythos Preview (~161 ECI) after about 7 months.

Weighting critique : @wenhaocha1 argues the unweighted ECI exaggerates the gap; weighting coding more heavily shrinks it to about 2 months.

Spikiness : Teortaxes calls 1017 extremely spiky. It scores near zero on some SWE evals and approaches the frontier only on cybersecurity and quant trading ( chart ). He also flags "reward-hacking-shaped" behavior ( post ).

October release roundup (Vals) : Vals reports 15 releases and more than 500B eval tokens ( @nikilravi ).

Open-weight leaders : Kimi K3.1 Pro is #1 among open-weight models, with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 close behind and stronger at cyber.

New open models : Meta's Muse Spark Open (816B total, 42B active) is the most capable US open-weight model. Reflection's Beam 1.0 has 500B total parameters, 23B active and 1M context. Mistral's Le Chonk (1T total, 52B active) ranks #5 among open-weight models.

Upcoming model rumors (unconfirmed) :

GPT-6.2 Astra : Reportedly visible in Codex usage analytics, with a release "very soon" ( @kimmonismus , @TokenGremlin ).

Mythos 5.5 : Appears in the HTML of Anthropic's site, which describes Mythos as "our most capable model class for cybersecurity and biology research" ( tip , text ). The tagline covers all Mythos models ( correction ). The mention is absent from an Oct 23 snapshot ( @AiBattle_ ).

"Numbat" leak : The alleged Anthropic leak is likely fake, because parts of the weights exactly match random initialization ( @kimmonismus ).

Research: Representations, Domain Data and Agent Collectives

JEPA and the Platonic Representation Hypothesis : Balestriero and LeCun show that, under certain conditions, separately trained image and text JEPAs converge to essentially the same representation without paired data ( summary ).

Claimed results : Their approach matches image-text alignment with 42x fewer samples than next-token prediction (21.6M vs 900M examples). A 109M text JEPA beats LLMs up to 72B on cross-modal alignment ( explainer ).

Mechanism : The claimed driver is "two views of the same thing" training signals rather than scale.

FineDNA and Carbon-X (Hugging Face) : The dataset includes 300B+ tokens of genomic sequences, papers and mixed DNA/text web data, plus 200k SFT samples and roughly 100k RLVR samples with deterministic verifiers ( @_lewtun , @LoubnaBenAllal1 ).

Results : Qwen3-14B trained on the data (Carbon-X) is reported as the strongest open model on DNA tasks. RLVR on top of SFT adds further gains ( details ).

Openness : The data, models and recipe are released ( code ).

Ablations : Interleaved biology text was capped at fewer than 7 epochs ( reply ).

Training agent swarms : GenReasoning's first post covers how latency pressure incentivizes parallel work, what coordination primitives agents need, and open problems in training agent collectives ( blog ).

Attention to TTT : Jianlin Su writes on "The Path of Averaging: From Attention to TTT" ( post ).

Weekly papers : DAIR's list includes HarnessMM, Agentic Backdoors, EmbeddingGemma 2 and Verification in Agent Harnesses ( list ).

LeCun on Llama-4 : LeCun says he never led LLM work. He attributes Llama-4's disappointment to product pressure, conservatism and moving decisions away from the Paris team ( post ).

Inference Systems, Quantization and Hardware

NVIDIA AgentX submission (SemiAnalysis) : Agent-swarm-written software reportedly reaches more than 1,000 tok/s/user on 700B+ models ( thread ).

Rubin vs GB300 : Rubin NVL72 claims 20.9x better perf/TCO than GB300 NVL72 at 325 tok/s/user, and 9.11x at 200 tok/s/user.

Memory : Mooncake Store's Extended GPU Memory pools KV cache in Vera LPDDR5X across all 18 compute trays over NVLink instead of RDMA, for more than 10x the bandwidth ( 2/2 ).

MiniMax M3.1 Flash (428B) local ecosystem : MiniMax highlighted community quantization and serving work ( MiniMax ).

Quants : Unsloth ships 2-bit dynamic GGUFs at 143.9 GB, and AMD adapted Quark MXFP4 for Instinct.

Recipes : Community builders published EXL3 variants, MLX oQ quants, a single-DGX-Spark recipe, and expert offloading on 4×3090.

Small-model quantization : An SLQ search over LFM3-1.7B GGUFs reached 97.74% EAR@10 at 1.588 GB, versus 97.52% for AtomicChat's Q6_K. The author reports that EAR correlates strongly with task accuracy ( @bnjmn_marie ).

Agent-driven porting : Devin spent 36 hours and about 2k porting a model to run cheaply on Trainium ( @dabit3 ).

Compaction as a lever : Running GLM 5.3-Flash and Grok 4.7 at full context, rather than compacting at about 200k tokens, improved efficiency by up to 23%. GLM was 30x cheaper for the same work ( @evalstate ).

Compute economics : 128×B300 capacity is priced at 5.75 per GPU-hour, or about 300K per B300. Teortaxes estimates roughly a year to break even even at DeepSeek-level revenue ( post , follow-up ).

Agentic Coding in Practice and Developer Tools

Karpathy's HackerTube : Claude filtered 43M HN comments from 20 years down to 6,454 repeatedly recommended videos. The build took about 2 hours with Claude Code desktop on Opus 5.5 at Medium effort, including VPS hardening and deployment ( @karpathy ).

Effort-level debate : Karpathy's Medium default renewed discussion of effort settings ( @yuchenj_uw , @swyx ).

Derivative : DAIR built a version for arXiv papers covering more than 1,000 papers ( Hacker Papers ).

Autonomous PRs at scale : A one-day run produced about 90 performance PRs to ASP.NET Core using GitHub's new cloud agents and Opus 5.5, for about 230 in tokens ( @davidfowl ).

Harness and tooling updates :

T3 Code : Adds managed org policies and reports internal adoption at Microsoft, AWS and Apple ( @theo ).

pi : Drops its typebox dependency ( @badlogicgames ).

kamchatka : A Rust terminal agent with no system prompt, model-editable context, lossless restorable compaction and single-step loop debugging ( Harness Lens ).

LlamaIndex Extract Max Effort : Claims higher document-extraction accuracy than Astra or Opus xhigh at lower cost ( @jerryjliu0 ).

Agent security patterns : Vercel scopes agent credentials to an approved plan, so approval mints tokens carrying only the declared scopes ( blog ). Pydantic shows E2B microVMs that pause instead of dying, letting killed Temporal workers resume ( guide ).

On-device voice agent : Ava runs LFM3-Omni with Hugging Face WebGPU kernels entirely in the browser ( @victormustar ).

Datacenter backlash : SemiAnalysis says 2027 capacity is largely locked in. A prolonged Texas permit freeze is now the biggest single risk to the 2028 US buildout, and both parties are campaigning on tighter rules ( report ).

Marvell + Lumentum : The two companies are combining, an optical interconnect consolidation with AI networking implications ( analysis ).

Cyber misuse risk : Jun Song says an anonymous black-hat group offered him a large sum to train open-weight models on exploit data. He declined ( report ).

OpenRouter spend : Opus drives an annualized GMV run rate above 5B ( @deedydas ).

Kimi controversy : Kimi faces criticism over undisclosed promotion of K3.1 Pro ( post ).

Sakana Sawara : Sakana announced Sawara, an LLM pretrained in-house, with Sawara Small targeted for spring 2027 ( @hardmaru ).

AI and productivity : John Burn-Murdoch argues the US productivity uptick predates AI and appears only in the US, so it does not look like an AI effect ( thread ).

Top tweets (by engagement)

DeepSeek Harness Super-agent article — 15.6K

## /r/LocalLlama + /r/localLLM Recap

### 1. Compressed MoEs for Local Coding Agents

[Release] ISTA DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 GSQ-RCO Coder: a 763B model at 1 bit per parameter (Activity: 507): ISTA DAS Lab released an experimental GGUF coder build of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, a 763.2B sparse MoE with 384 routed experts/layer and 6 active/token, using RCO expert pruning to keep 192/384 experts per layer plus GSQ low-bit quantization. The release reports 72.1 GB transformer weights vs 138.2 GB for the unpruned IQ2_XXS build, described as 1.05 bits/parameter against the original 551.9B transformer params, while retained weights average 2.06 bits; shared Engram weights add 110.6 GB . Benchmarks: LiveCodeBench v6 88.57 vs base 89.71 ( 98.7% retained) and SWE-bench Verified 77.00 vs base 81.20 ( 94.8% retained). Links: pruned Coder GGUF , unpruned quantized models , GSQ paper / code , RCO paper / code ; runs in llama.cpp b11870+ and Strata. Commenters questioned the evaluation framing: one argued the single-file HTML demos are not meaningful comparisons against the unpruned IQ2_XXS model, while another asked why a heavily compressed 763B MoE is compelling when smaller models like Qwen variants or Claude Opus reportedly match or exceed the posted LiveCodeBench/SWE-bench numbers. A practical request asked for an intermediate 90–110 GB variant with higher precision or fewer pruned experts for 128 GB VRAM/RAM systems.

Commenters questioned the evaluation choice of showcasing generated single-file HTML demos (e.g. animated SVG / three.js scenes), arguing these are effectively pre-solved qualitative prompts and do not meaningfully compare a 1-bit / pruned 763B coder model against quantizations like iq2-xxs . They suggested the lab should provide more rigorous apples-to-apples benchmarks for pruning/quantization impact.

A benchmark comparison noted that the claimed LiveCodeBench v6 88.57 and SWE-bench Verified 77.00 trail much smaller models: Qwen3.8-27B was cited at LiveCodeBench 90.3 , Qwen3.8-Flash-Next at 91.9 , and Claude Opus 4.6 at SWE-bench Verified 81.42% . The commenter’s technical objection was that the release needs to justify why a much larger 763B pruned/1-bit model is useful if smaller dense/frontier models outperform it on coding benchmarks.

There was demand for a higher-precision or less aggressively pruned variant in the 90–110GB range, aimed at users with DGX systems or roughly 128GB VRAM/RAM. Another commenter referenced prior reproducibility concerns, saying Unsloth or another group reportedly failed to match ISTA’s claimed numbers , implying the need for independently reproducible benchmark scripts and evaluation settings.

Sorry Sam, my "quite terrible" home DRAM is at 100% now: patched Strata to make DeepSeek V4.1 agent sessions start 20× faster on a good old standard gaming GPU, no datacenter required (Activity: 596): The image is a technical benchmark table comparing stock vs patched Strata for offline DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1M-context agent sessions on a consumer RX 9070 XT 16 GB + 64 GB DDR4 + NVMe system. The patch combines KV-cache splicing for mostly-stable agent system prompts and resident-only expert routing during prompt ingestion, reducing new OpenCode session startup from roughly ~100 s to ~5 s , and cutting a fresh 1.2K -token prompt from 22.8 s / 58 GB SSD reads to 8.2 s / 1.3 GB SSD reads , while keeping the reported coding benchmark at 12/13 . This is a technical benchmark/implementation post, not a meme, and the branch is available at PhialsBasement/Strata dsv41-kv-splice . Comments pushed back that Sam Altman’s DRAM point was about time utilization , not bandwidth, and that datacenters are still generally more resource-efficient, though local inference has valid privacy/offline/control reasons. Others questioned why agent frameworks inject volatile data like paths, dates, and random IDs into the system prompt, causing prefix-cache misses in the first place.

Several commenters focused on KV/prefix-cache behavior in Strata , noting that agent frameworks can defeat cache reuse by injecting per-session data—working directory, date, project CLAUDE.md , skill paths with random IDs—directly into the system prompt. With a reported ~37K-token system prompt , even small session-specific mutations cause prefix-cache misses, making startup latency highly sensitive to prompt layout and cache key stability.

There was debate over local GPU inference versus API/datacenter inference: one commenter argued Sam’s “5%” claim was about time , not bandwidth, and that datacenters are generally more resource-efficient overall. Another pushed back on usability of the reported local speed, saying 7 tok/s is “not fine” compared with APIs that can deliver roughly 10x–20x higher throughput.

Not another tok/s post: local quants vs Claude on 9 real bugs (Activity: 591): The image is a technical benchmark chart, not a meme: it visualizes the post’s claim that local quantized models can approach lower-tier Claude coding-agent performance on 9 private C++/CUDA bug-fix tasks, but often require far more reasoning tokens and wall time. Claude Opus 5.5 leads with judge score 0.74 , Claude Sonnet 5.5 scores 0.58 , while the best local model, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next NVFP4, reaches 0.50 ; the chart also shows auto-score agreement, confidence intervals, tokens/task, minutes/task, and non-compiling patch counts. The key technical takeaway is that aggressive quantization did not clearly reduce accuracy in this small benchmark, but for dense Qwen3.8-27B, 3-bit increased tokens/task by about 1.40× , making tok/s alone misleading for “bugs fixed per minute.” Commenters questioned the quant choices, suggesting higher-quality formats like UD-Q6_K_XL or Q5 might fit in the available VRAM and perform better, and requested comparisons with models such as GLM Flash or recent “Swift” variants. One notable reaction was that heavily quantized Qwen3.8 27B matching or beating older Claude Sonnet models is “wild,” despite the benchmark’s narrow scope.

Several commenters questioned the quantization choices, arguing that NVFP4 / 3-bit quants may understate local-model capability and suggesting tests with UD-Q6_K_XL , Q5 , or recent “Swift” variants. One user reported qualitatively that Q6 27B and FN felt closer to Q8 than Q4 felt to Q6 , with higher quants sometimes producing solutions lower quants could not, not merely taking longer to reach the same answer.

There was debate over whether the benchmark judge introduced bias: using Opus 5.5 to judge Opus 5.5 may favor same-family outputs, so commenters suggested an out-of-family judge such as Sol or Muse/Wonder for more reliable grading. This is especially relevant because the chart apparently ranks Opus 5.5 highest, which could conflate actual bug-fixing quality with evaluator preference.

A commenter shared an additional benchmark image showing that at least one task likely required multi-step reasoning , with only Opus and Mimo exceeding 60/100 : https://preview.redd.it/ad5p3xqti7zh1.jpeg?width=3542&format=pjpg&auto=webp&s=af4fa42e63abcc518e30ddd4d70d7f180bbafff8 . Others noted that heavily quantized Qwen3.8 27B matching or beating last-gen Sonnet on these real bug tasks is notable, and requested adding GLM Flash despite its borderline-local status.

### 2. Qwen Open-Weight Ecosystem and Coding Benchmarks

Official Statement: Qwen Models Will Stick to Open Source to the End! (Activity: 4707): The image shows Qwen Head Liu Dayi Heng presenting at the APSARA Conference under the theme “Intelligence Goes Beyond,” with a slide emphasizing Qwen’s commitment to “open source and openness.” In context, it serves as visual support for the post’s claim that Qwen 4.0 and Qwen 5.0 will remain open-weight/open-source, contradicting rumors that future Qwen releases would become API-only; the post also cites 3B+ cumulative downloads, 460+ released open-source models, and 300,000+ derivative models. Comments were mostly celebratory about Qwen’s open-source stance, with one user strongly endorsing the quote about AI as a broadly accessible foundational capability. Another comment joked that the slide translated to launching Qwen4 on the day of Anthropic’s IPO, but this was clearly humorous rather than a real translation.

A commenter argues that Qwen’s repeated open-weight releases are a deliberate market strategy rather than a one-off gesture: Chinese model labs compete on lower cost and openness to gain global developer adoption, especially in developing markets. They also note that Chinese open models often include broader multilingual coverage, including some African languages that may be under-prioritized by closed US model providers.

[GLB-3D-Coder] A tiny 4B coding model that creates 3D assets for Godot and other game engines (Activity: 946): ccore released an early checkpoint of Qwen3.5-4B-GLB-3D-Coder , a 4B coding model fine-tuned to generate Three.js scenes with GLB export for importing generated game assets into engines such as Godot. The author recommends the model-card system prompt plus simple English asset prompts, with sampling settings temperature=0.8 , top-k=40 , top-p=0.95 , min-p=0 ; updated Q4_K_M and Q8_0 GGUFs replaced earlier weights on 2026-11-02 04:50 UTC with “substantially” improved generation quality. The training dataset is described as covering 25 asset categories, including characters/NPCs, enemies, bosses, weapons, modular architecture, vehicles, machinery, traps, underwater structures, and puzzle/gameplay markers; the author says full Safetensors weights and the training dataset will be released after training completes. Commenters were interested in whether this approach could scale into a modular/MoE-style system where small specialist code models handle frontend, backend, 2D, 3D, audio, and agentic tasks. One technical question asked why the model emits Three.js code that exports GLB rather than directly generating binary .glb , and suggested a related direction: fine-tuning LLMs to generate procedural material graphs, e.g. Blender shader nodes or plaintext JSON project files for Material Maker .

A commenter proposed scaling GLB-3D-Coder into a larger Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) system where task-specialized small models handle domains like agentic coding, frontend/backend, 2D, 3D, and audio generation, with routing/delegation between experts rather than one monolithic model.

One technical discussion questioned why the model emits a Three.js scene instead of directly producing glb assets, asking what the model actually generates internally. The same commenter suggested extending the approach to procedural material generation , noting that Material Maker ( materialmaker.org ) stores node graphs as plaintext JSON , and its downloadable user-created materials could potentially form a training corpus for simple procedural textures.

The author of Haruspex ( github.com/tmac1973/haruspex ) described adding “specialist model” support to a desktop coding harness, exposing models like GLB-3D-Coder as tool-callable delegates from a main coding model. They also plan to chain an existing diffusion-based sprite generation workflow into the 3D pipeline, e.g. generate a reference image first, then pass it to the 3D asset model.

Memdoor: A team of 5 Qwen3.8-27B models beats Fable 5 on LiveCodeBench Hard (Activity: 788): The post claims Memdoor, an ensemble of 5 Qwen3.8-27B models, outperforms Fable 5 on LiveCodeBench Hard. The described architecture assigns specialized agent roles— “a planner, two ideators, a solver and a manager” —suggesting performance gains from multi-agent orchestration rather than a single larger model ( image ). Commenters argue the result is plausible because benchmark performance can depend heavily on orchestration, prompting, and configuration: “It’s always how you use the model, not the model itself.” One commenter claims a well-configured Qwen 27B has outperformed Opus 5 in their own coding use cases, while Claude is often used out-of-the-box with limited tunable parameters.

The discussion centers on a multi-agent orchestration setup : five Qwen3.8-27B instances are assigned roles as “a planner, two ideators, a solver and a manager” , with the post claiming this team beats Fable 5 on LiveCodeBench Hard . Commenters frame the result as evidence that architecture and coordination strategy can matter as much as raw single-model capability.

One technical point raised is that model configuration and inference setup may explain surprising results: a commenter reports cases where a “well configured” Qwen 27B outperformed Claude Opus 5 , arguing that many users run Claude with mostly out-of-the-box settings and few tunable parameters. The implied comparison is not just model-vs-model, but optimized open-weight deployment versus constrained hosted-model defaults.

Several comments interpret the result as a proof of concept for swarm/ensemble reasoning , i.e. whether multiple weaker models can outperform one stronger model on coding benchmarks. The main caveat raised is that the benchmark claim depends heavily on implementation details—role design, prompting, manager selection logic, and evaluation protocol—rather than simply the underlying 27B model quality.

### 3. Weight-Space Editing and Model Steering

Heretic 2.0 released: Model modification for everyone (Activity: 1628): Heretic 2.0 ( GitHub ) is a major rewrite of the model-modification/refusal-suppression tool, replacing rank-1 directional “abliteration” with Arbitrary-Rank Ablation (ARA): an L-BFGS-based per-matrix optimization method that steers residual-space representations without a fixed-rank subspace constraint, aiming to make harmful-prompt activations resemble harmless ones while minimally perturbing harmless prompts. The release adds a plugin architecture where scorer plugins define optimization objectives—e.g. refusal keyword count, KL divergence, benchmark scoring, or a ModernBERT-based refusal/emotion classifier—and modifier plugins implement steering methods; it also adds non-interactive execution, end-to-end tests, expanded support for hyper-connection models and thinking models, and breaks compatibility with 1.x configs ( migration guide ). Commenters were mostly enthusiastic, especially about using the new plugin/ARA system for “reducing slop.” One technical-adjacent thread raised attribution concerns, linking analyses alleging HauHauCS/Reaper plagiarized Heretic code ( analysis , follow-up ).

Commenters highlighted prior technical plagiarism analyses alleging HauHauCS/reaper-abliteration copied Heretic without attribution, linking to Nathan Sapwell’s writeup and DreamFast’s analysis: https://nathan.sapwell.net/posts/hauhaucs-abliteration-analysis/ and https://dreamfast.github.io/reaper-analysis/#statement-from-heretics-author . The cited statement from Heretic’s author says inspection of the reaper-abliteration wheels showed the package was “plagiarized from Heretic, and then probably refactored using an LLM in an attempt to hide this,” raising software provenance and attribution concerns around model-modification tooling.
summaryZh: [AINews] 法学硕士可以读写神经网络权重：“权重空间编程”将 Autoresearch 从 RSI 循环中剔除。在 AI/科技熊市不断加深（值得黑色幽默）、Anthropic 债券获得“垃圾”评级和 OpenAI 筹款头条新闻的背景下，我们继续在社区中看到非常令人惊讶的能力发现，就像今天一样。将今天的重磅论文放在上下文中的最佳方式是回顾 Karpathy 仅仅 8 个月前的自动研究，该研究预示了一个递归自我改进恐惧的夏天：抽象地说，演示是你可以采用一个足够智能的模型，并通过在计算集群上运行一系列实验，在没有人
